children: Boeing investors face a fresh problem with the company's troubled 737 MAX jet-which could prompt volatile trading in shares this coming week.

Saturday, The Wall Street Journal reported a MAX software glitch that can affect landing after an initial missed approach. Boeing notified airlines of the problem in late August. The company, its customers, and regulators have been assessing the problem and whether it poses a safety risk.

"Last month, we informed all 737 operators about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario," said Boeing in an emailed statement to Barron's. "We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases. Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue."
The Federal Aviation Administration didn't immediately respond to Barron's request for comment.

Investors are highly attuned to MAX problems. Faulty flight control software led to two deadly MAX crashes in 2018 and 2019, leaving the plane grounded worldwide for almost two years while Boeing worked on a fix. In January 2024, poor production quality led to an emergency door plug blowing out of an Alaska Air flight, necessitating an emergency landing.
The turmoil led to management turnover, which culminated in the hiring of veteran aerospace executive Kelly Ortberg. He took over as CEO of Boeing in August 2024.

Under Ortberg, Boeing has made steady progress improving production and approving new plane models. After the door plug incident, Boeing was allowed by the FAA to make 38 MAX jets a month in 2024. Now, it is authorized to make 47 a month. What's more, the FAA recently certified the shorter version of the MAX for commercial service in August.

Boeing is still waiting for the longest version of the 737 MAX to be approved for commercial service. It is also working on certifying the huge, twin-aisle 777X. It's unclear how the software glitch will impact the regulatory process-but it won't help.

MAX issues, Covid, supply-chain constraints, labor unrest, production quality, and high oil prices have battered Boeing shares over the years. Boeing stock was north of $440 in March 2019, before the second tragic MAX crash. It closed below $200 a share on Friday.

Boeing investors hope that plane production will yield 800-plus jet deliveries in 2028, which should translate into some $10 billion in free cash flow. In the long run, changes to those delivery and free cash flow estimates matter most for the stock. But in the short run, shares could see more volatile trading: investors just can't be sure how severe the new MAX software issue is yet. And investors hate uncertainty.
About 2,400 MAX jets have been delivered since the plane's first delivery in 2017, and Boeing has more than 4,700 unfilled orders.
